what_its_for: Ixazomib is a cancer medicine used to treat multiple myeloma (a type of blood cancer). It is used together with two other medicines called lenalidomide and dexamethasone in patients who have already received at least one prior treatment for their cancer.
how_to_take: Swallow the capsule whole with water. Do not open, crush, or chew the capsule. Take it on an empty stomach — at least 1 hour before eating or at least 2 hours after eating. Always take it on the same day of the week and at about the same time. Handle the capsule carefully; if the powder inside touches your skin, wash the area well with soap and water right away.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 4 mg taken by mouth once a week on the same day each week (for example, every Monday). You will take it on Days 1, 8, and 15 of a 28-day treatment cycle. Your doctor may lower your dose if you have side effects or certain health conditions such as kidney or liver problems.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and your next scheduled dose is more than 3 days away (72 hours or more), take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If your next scheduled dose is less than 3 days away (fewer than 72 hours), skip the missed dose and take your next dose on your regular day. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store ixazomib capsules at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep them in the original packaging to protect them from moisture. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking St. John's Wort or other strong enzyme-inducing supplements or herbal products, as they can make ixazomib less effective. Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting ixazomib. Avoid becoming pregnant while taking this medicine — it can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Both men and women must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 90 days after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience any of the following: severe diarrhea, constipation, nausea, or vomiting that is hard to control; a rash, especially one that is severe, blistering, or peeling; swelling of your arms, legs, hands, or feet (peripheral edema); tingling, numbness, burning, or pain in your hands or feet (nerve problems); signs of a low platelet count such as unusual bruising or bleeding; signs of infection such as fever, chills, or cough; severe back pain or any new back pain; yellowing of the skin or eyes, or dark urine (possible liver problems); or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Ixazomib works throughout your treatment cycle. It may take several weeks to months before your doctors can measure how well the medicine is working through blood tests and other checks. It is important to keep taking it exactly as prescribed and attend all follow-up appointments, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Your doctor may lower your starting dose if you have severe kidney disease or if you are on dialysis. Liver problems: Your doctor may lower your starting dose if you have moderate or severe liver disease. Older adults (65 and over): Ixazomib can be used in older adults, but side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and low platelets may be more noticeable — let your doctor know right away. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do NOT use ixazomib if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It can harm your unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant and male patients with female partners who can become pregnant must use effective contraception during treatment and for 90 days after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine.
